findings.claim: Nobody ever looked at the button that completes the order on variant B.
findings.evidence: On the review step, “Confirm purchase · $147.95” sits below the fold. Of the 9 people who got that far, 0 looked at it. On variant A the same control was seen by 12 of 12, after 0.4 s.

findings.claim: 5 of 9 people who reached the review step on variant B gave up there instead of going on.
findings.evidence: That is 56% of the people who got that far, and 5 of the 11 who gave up anywhere on variant B gave up here.

findings.claim: Only 2 of 12 people who reached the payment step on variant A ever looked at “CVC”, so it did no work for the rest of them.
findings.evidence: It is one of the things the task needs somebody to use. 17% of the 12 people who got that far looked at it at all, and it held none of their attention across the step.

findings.claim: Not one of the 9 people who reached the review step on variant B ever looked at “Need help?”, so it did no work at all.
findings.evidence: It is one of the things the task needs somebody to use. 0% of the 9 people who got that far looked at it at all, and it held none of their attention across the step.

findings.claim: 1 of 12 people who reached the review step on variant A ended there with no order placed, and leaving was not their choice.
findings.evidence: All 1 stopped on that step with the task unfinished and the product at fault — a failure, not someone choosing to leave. Each of them recorded the same reason: The session ended on the "review" step with the task not done. The primary action in "A-review-complete" was fixated 6 times, first 22.5 s in, but never clicked..

findings.claim: 1 of 24 people could not be simulated to the end, and are excluded from both figures.
findings.evidence: Our own browser automation gave up on the payment step (1 person on variant B). This is a weakness of the simulation, never evidence against your checkout.
